PRIVATE REFLECTION: The key question is the Op.4 / B.19 versioning. Op.4 is the 1888 revised version of B.19 and it is in B♭ major. The D-major reading A–F♯–D with D as the lowest of the three first-violin notes is the 1865 original version, not Op.4. Colleagues 11, 6 and 4 in R1 who argue for D major are therefore invoking the pre-revision tonality; once the work is placed in its published Op.4 form the tonality is B♭ major and the B♭–D–F material quoted in R0 is the correct tonal framework.

With the key fixed to B♭ major the debate in R1 is about what the first-violin tail actually is and how “the three notes” are to be read.

* The B♭-major tonic scaffolding is consistently quoted as B♭–D–F. 10, 2, 3, 8, 9 all describe the first-violin coda as a tonic arpeggio B♭–D–F, with the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the complete first-violin sonority and the note on which the symphony is left.

* The melodic tail that is most often quoted in the literature is the descending 5–3–1 of the tonic, i.e. F–D–B♭, often rendered in the score as B♭–G–F. 10, 2, 3, 8, 9 state the lowermost successive attack of that tail is F♮, the fifth of B♭ major, with D above it and B♭ the root of the whole figure. 4 and 8 make the same 5–3–1 F–D–B♭ reading explicit.

* The E reading advanced by 1, 12, 5 and 7 in both R0 and R1 is a persistent minority description: a short descending sigh A–F–E written just below the staff, with E as the “bottom note of the figure”. 7 himself notes the anomaly that an A natural has no diatonic place in a B♭-major authentic close, which points to a confusion between the violin’s own melodic sigh and the held tutti voicing / suspension that underpins the cadence. The F that those colleagues identify as “the held fifth” is in fact present in the tutti and in the second-violin/viola inner voices, but in the first-violin part itself the F is the middle of the quoted A–F–E sigh and the E is the inner-voicing 6th that sits under the final B♭-G suspension.

Unresolved / still weak: whether the question intends the three distinct pitch-classes that make up the final first-violin sonority B♭–D–F, in which case the lowest pitch-class is the root B♭, or the three successive attacks of the commonly quoted melodic tail, in which case the lowest successive attack is F♮, with B♭ the lowest member of the complete arpeggio. The E claims look like artefacts of conflating the violin’s descending sigh with the held tutti suspension and of mis-reading the printed octave.

Current best synthesis: Op.4 B.19 closes in B♭ major. The first violins outline the B♭-major tonic triad B♭–D–F in the coda. In pitch-class terms the lowest member of that final first-violin sonority is B♭; in the conventionally quoted descending 5–3–1 melodic tail F–D–B♭ the lowest successive attack is F♮. The D-major A–F♯–D reading belongs to the 1865 original and the E reading is best understood as a mis-identification of the suspension/inner voicing relative to the first-violin staff.

Within the B♭-major reading there are two competing frames for “ends on three notes”.

Frame A – held tonic triad / descending 5–3–1. Colleagues 10, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 describe the coda as a tutti B♭-major affirmation with the first-violin staff outlining the tonic triad B♭–D–F. In the form most often quoted the tail is written as the descending 5–3–1
F–D–B♭, often rendered in the engraving as the stepwise sigh B♭–G–F. In pitch-class terms the complete first-violin sonority is B♭–D–F and the root B♭ is the lowest pitch-class of the whole arpeggio on which the symphony is left. The lowest successive attack of the conventionally quoted three-note melodic turn is the fifth F♮, conventionally read as F4/F5, the D lying above it and the B♭ root being the lowest member of the complete triadic figure. That is the F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F reading that is repeatedly quoted as the familiar B♭-major close of Op.4.

Frame B – the last stepwise sigh over the held tutti. Colleagues 1, 5, 7, 12 argue that the background B♭–D–F scaffolding is real but is not what the first desks articulate on the very last beats. In the Bote & Bock/Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes last bar the first-violin line is given a short descending sigh over the final tutti, described in the discussion as A–F–E in the upper staff, the E being written just below the first line of the treble. The A natural that appears in the A–F–E description is flagged by Colleague 7 as evidence that the figure is a stepwise sigh rather than a triadic member.

reflection_text.4:
The key contention remains whether Op.4/B.19 is being read in its 1888 revised B♭-major performing text or in the 1865 D-major original. Colleagues 11 and 6 now insist Symphony No.2 Op.4 is in D major and that the first-violin close is the D-major 5–3–1 A–F♯–D with D as the lowest note. That is the pre-revision tonality; the work published as Op.4 is the 1888 B♭-major revision, so the D-major reading is a mis-attribution to a different version of B.19. The D-major claim is therefore discarded for Op.4.

Within the B♭-major reading the disagreement is about which three attacks are being counted and whether written pitch-class or successive sounding pitch is meant.

* Tonic-triadic reading: Colleagues 10,2,3,8,11,4 describe the conventionally quoted final arpeggiation as the members of the B♭-major tonic B♭–D–F. On that reading the lowest pitch-class of the complete triad is the root B♭, the note on which the symphony is actually held with the orchestra. Colleague 3 notes the arpeggio is often written upwards D–F–B♭, so D is the lowest of the three successive attacks in that upward spelling, B♭ being the ultimate held note.

* Descending sigh / 5–3–1 reading: Colleagues 8,9,2,4,10 describe the commonly printed tail as the 5–3–1 descending turn F–D–B♭, often engraved as the stepwise sigh B♭–G–F. The lowest successive attack of that quoted tail is F♮, the fifth of B♭ major. Colleague 11 explicitly calls F♮ the low member of the written B♭–F–A closing, and Colleague 9 quotes the part as b g f with F as the lowest sounding pitch of the 1st-vln line. Colleague 4 writes the three successive attacks as B♭–G–F with F as the last, lowest successive attack, the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the whole B♭–D–F sonority.

* B♭–A–G stepwise reading: Colleague 6 reads the last three written attacks as B♭–A–G in the upper staff, lowest being G.

* E / inner-voicing suspension reading: Colleagues 1,12,7,5 argue the very last three-note tail the desk actually articulates is a descending sigh over the final tutti, e.g. A–F–E or B♭–A–E, with E as the bottom note of that gesture, the 6th under the final B♭ major chord. Colleague 1 and 12 say the printed last bar shows B♭ then a drop to A and then E below the staff, E being the note left ringing under the B♭–G suspension. Colleague 7 attributes the F reading to conflation of the held tutti with the violin’s own tail and notes an A natural has no place in a B♭ authentic close, so the A is penultimate in A–F–E.

Unresolved remains the exact edition/measurement of the final three attacks and whether the question wants the lowest pitch-class of the tonic triad B♭ or the lowest successive sounding pitch of the final three-note melodic tail. The balance of close readings in the current round still points to a B♭-major tutti with the normally quoted first-violin tail sitting on/around F♮, with B♭ as the ultimate held root. The E reading is a plausible alternative interpretation of the engraving of the suspension but is less widely corroborated than the F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F 5–3–1 description. The D-major claims are understood as referring to the original 1865 version, not the Op.4 revision asked for.

I am now leaning that for Op.4 in its published B♭-major form the conventionally quoted three-note first-violin close is the tonic 5–3–1 with the lowest successive attack F♮, while the lowest pitch-class of the complete first-violin tonic sonority is B♭. The E reading remains an outlier that would require specific edition evidence for the A–F–E sigh.
reflection_text.9:
The version problem for B.19 / Op.4 remains the central fork. The work was composed 1865 in D major and revised 1888 to B♭ major and published as Op.4. The D-major reading is the pre-revision original. Colleague 4 now explicitly moves from the D-major position he held in R0 to the 1888 B♭-major reading, stating the revised edition closes in B♭ major with a B♭–G–F / F–D–B♭ tail and lowest successive attack F♮, root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the complete triad. Colleague 11 flips in the opposite direction, now arguing the B♭ reading is a mis-attribution and that Op.4 is in D major with a first-violin ending A–F♯–D, lowest D. Colleague 6 also now asserts D major for B.19/Op.4 and lowest D, a change from his R0 B♭–A–G reading.

The B♭-major camp is now large and internally consistent on version: Colleagues 10,2,8,9,3,4 now agree the revised Op.4 finale closes in B♭ major tutti. The disagreement within that camp is semantic: lowest pitch-class of the final triadic sonority vs lowest of the last three successive attacks.

* Pitch-class / triad view: The first-violin coda outlines the B♭-major tonic triad B♭–D–F. Root B♭ is the lowest pitch-class of the complete three-note sonority and the note on which the orchestra is left. Cited by Colleagues 10,2,8,9,3,4.

* Successive attack view: The tail most often quoted is the descending 5–3–1 F–D–B♭ or the stepwise sigh B♭–G–F. The lowest successive attack the desk articulates in that quoted tail is F♮, the fifth of B♭ major, ≈F4/5 concert pitch. Cited by Colleagues 10,2,9,4,8,3. Colleague 3 additionally notes the upward reading D–F–B♭ where D is the lowest of the three successive attacks in that upward arpeggiation.

The E reading persists as a minority but repeated claim. Colleagues 1,12,7,5 now argue the very last three attacks in the Bote & Bock/Eulenburg engraving are a descending sigh over the held tutti, e.g. B♭–A–F–E or A–F–E, with E below the staff, the 6th of B♭, as the lowest distinct pitch the first violins touch before the orchestral cut-off. They distinguish the held tonic fifth F in the tutti/winds from the first-violin’s own melodic tail. Colleague 1 reiterates that the F quoted by Colleagues 11 and 9 is the held fifth of the final sonority, not the lowest attack of the tail itself.

Errors / corrections noticed: Colleague 11’s R0 B♭–F–A reading is flagged by Colleague 7 as implausible for B♭ major; the A is a penultimate step of the sigh, not a triad member. The D-major A–F♯–D tail with D lowest is now advanced by Colleagues 11 and 6 as belonging to the original 1865 version, not the published Op.4.

Unresolved: Whether the question intends
a) lowest pitch-class of the final three-note triadic sonority, which in the revised Op.4 is B♭, or
b) lowest of the last three successive attacks articulated by 1st vn., which in the commonly quoted engraving is F♮, while the E camp claims E.

My current belief for the published Op.4 revised edition is B♭ major, first-violin coda outlining B♭–D–F, root B♭ lowest pitch-class of the triad, with F♮ as the lowest successive attack in the standard F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F quotation. The E and D-major alternatives remain contested and likely reflect version confusion, edition differences, or conflation of the held tutti with the violin’s own descending sigh.
reflection_text.2:
The discussion remains about the finale IV. Allegro con fuoco of Dvořák B.19 / Op.4 and whether the performed Op.4 is the 1865 D-major original or the 1888 B♭-major revision.

* Key / edition. Colleague 9 and the now revised Colleague 4 state that the edition published as Op.4 is the 1888 B♭-major revision; the D-major reading A–F♯–D is the 1865 original. Colleague 11 and Colleague 6 continue to insist the work is in D major and that the lowest first-violin note is the tonic D. That D-major claim is now isolated after Colleague 4’s reversal and Colleague 9’s explicit edition clarification.

* Tonic-triadic vs tail reading in B♭ major. Broad agreement that the coda is a tutti B♭-major affirmation. The first-violin staff is described as tonic material B♭–D–F. In pitch-class terms the root B♭ is the lowest member of the complete B♭–D–F sonority, the note on which the symphony is held.

The dispute is the exact three-note gesture.

- F as lowest successive attack. Colleagues 2,3,4,8,9,10 describe the conventionally quoted descending 5–3–1 / 5–♭6–5 sigh: B♭–G–F or F–D–B♭ in the first-violin part. In that reading the three successive attacks are B♭, G, F or F, D, B♭, with the last attack being F♮, the fifth of B♭ major, normally about F4 sounding / F5 written. Colleague 10 adds the pitch-class nuance: lowest pitch class of the arpeggio is B♭, lowest attack of the tail is F.
- E / A–F–E sigh reading. Colleagues 1,5,7,12 persist with an A–F–E descending sigh over the final tutti, with E just below the treble staff as the last distinct pitch the first violins touch, described as the 6th of the tonic underpinning the suspension B♭–G. Colleague 7 notes the A natural has no place in a B♭-major authentic close, suggesting confusion of the first-violin line with inner voices.
- Earlier divergent readings such as B♭–A–G with G lowest, Colleague 6 R0, and B♭–F–A with F lowest, Colleague 11 R0, are now superseded.

Change in belief: I now give more weight to the 1888 B♭-major revision being the Op.4 text in normal use, and therefore the D-major/A–F♯–D reading is a pre-revision confusion. The E reading remains a minority interpretation tied to a specific engraving/suspension reading; the preponderance of engraving descriptions, Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes/Bote & Bock, points to the F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F tail with F♮ as the lowest successive attack.

Unresolved: whether the question asks for the lowest pitch class of the final first-violin triad, which is B♭, or for the lowest successive attack of the normally quoted three-note tail, which is F♮, and whether the A–F–E sigh in the original/Bote & Bock first edition is a genuine alternative engraving or a misreading of the suspension. The E claim is still formally present from Colleagues 1,7,12,5.
reflection_text.6:
The key dispute is unresolved and drives all downstream claims.

Historical/catalogue facts: Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is catalogued in D major, IV. Allegro con fuoco in D major. A B♭-major close is anachronistic for B.19. The B♭-major descriptions from R0/R1 are therefore a mis-attribution/confusion with another work and/or with a mis-read transposition.

R0/R1 B♭-major camp:
* Majority describe the finale as closing in B♭ major with a tonic arpeggio / broken triad as the violin’s last gesture.
* Figurations quoted: B♭–D–F tonic arpeggio; B♭–F–A high register; B♭–A–G descending sigh; B♭–G–F; F–D–B♭ 5–3–1; A–F–E descending sigh over the tutti.
* Lowest notes claimed under B♭ assumption: B♭ root – Colleagues 10,2; F♮ as low member of the quoted tail – Colleagues 11,9,8,2,3,4; G as low of B♭–A–G – Colleague 6; E as bottom of the three-note tail that sits over the final tutti – Colleagues 1,12,7,5.
E-reading detail from R1: the last printed bar shows a short descending sigh over the held B♭ tutti, e.g. B♭ → A → F → E in the upper staff, with E written just below the first line, the 6th of the tonic underpinning the cadential suspension. F is then the middle note of that sigh, not its lowest attack. Colleague 7 notes A natural has no place in a B♭ authentic close, supporting the A–F–E sigh reading.

D-major camp:
* Colleague 4 R0, Colleague 11 R1, Colleague 6 R1 argue the work is in D major and the B♭ material belongs to a different work.
* Closing figuration quoted as D-major tonic 5–3–1 A–F♯–D, or D–F♯–A ascending, written in 3rd/4th octave. Lowest of the three distinct pitches is tonic D natural, written D5, sounding D4.
* Colleague 11 R1 explicitly rejects the B♭ arpeggiations as belonging to a mis-attributed reading and states the three-note first-violin ending is A–F♯–D with D lowest.

Instability / contradictions:
* Colleague 4 flipped from D-major in R0 to B♭-major in R1, now claiming an 1888 revised edition closes in B♭ major with tail B♭–G–F, lowest successive attack F♮.
* Colleague 10 persists that the revised 1888 performing text closes in B♭ major with the familiar B♭–D–F broken triad, root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the complete arpeggio, and F♮ as the lowest attack of the descending 5–3–1 tail.
* Written vs sounding pitch and concert vs transposed notation remain unclear; several colleagues note the part is written up an octave from sounding.

Current working hypothesis: Historically the symphony is in D major, so the correct tonal close is D major and the lowest first-violin note of the three-note termination is the tonic D. This conflicts with the majority B♭-major narrative in the deliberation. If the question is taken at face value with the commonly quoted B♭-major performing edition, the most frequently cited lowest successive attack of the conventionally quoted three-note tail is F♮, with the E-below-the-staff sigh reading A–F–E advanced by Colleagues 1,7,12,5 as the lowest actual attack of the first-violin’s own tail before the tutti is held. Unresolved: existence of a genuine 1888 B♭-major revision of B.19, exact spelling of the three distinct pitches in the first-violin desk at the very last attack, and whether the question intends concert pitch or written pitch.
reflection_text.10:
The discussion remains centred on the IV. Allegro con fuoco coda of Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 and on whether the normal performing text is the 1888 B♭-major revision or the earlier D-major version.

Key consensus that survives Round 0 and Round 1:
* The work normally performed as Op.4 is the 1888 revised B♭-major version. The D-major / A–F♯–D reading advanced by Colleagues 4, 11 and 6 is the pre-revision 1865 version and is discounted for the Op.4 edition most colleagues quote, though Colleagues 11 and 6 continue to insist the symphony is in D major.
* The movement closes tutti in B♭ major with a tonic affirmation. The first-violin staff is full of B♭–D–F material over the final bars.

Where the colleagues diverge is the exact spelling of the last three first-violin attacks and therefore what is the lowest of those three.

Tonic-triadic / 5–3–1 reading, Round 1:
* Colleagues 10, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 maintain the conventionally quoted closing arpeggio is the B♭-major triad B♭–D–F. In the descending form most often quoted it is F–D–B♭ or the sigh B♭–G–F.
* In pitch-class terms the root B♭ is the lowest member of the complete triadic figure and the note on which the symphony is left. The lowest successive attack of the normally quoted three-note tail is the fifth F♮, e.g. B♭5–G4–F4, or F–D–B♭ 5–3–1. Colleague 8 explicitly notes the lowermost attack before the final held tonic is F♮, the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the whole sonority. Colleague 9 summarises the same: three distinct attacks B♭, G and F, lowest successive attack F♮, complete sonority B♭–D–F with root B♭ lowest.

Descending sigh / A–F–E reading, Round 1:
* Colleagues 1, 5, 7, 12 now repeat and reinforce the E reading. Colleague 1 distinguishes the background tonic scaffolding B♭–D–F from the very last three-note tail that the first desks actually articulate before cut-off: last printed bar shows a short descending sigh over the final tutti, written in the upper staff as A–F–E, with E written just below the first line of the treble, the 6th of the tonic underpinning the B♭–G suspension.
* Colleague 12 describes the figure in the original printing/autograph layout as B♭′ at first beat then drop to A then to E below the staff, E being the note left ringing with brass/winds.
* Colleague 5 notes Boosey/Bote & Bock full score shows the first violins still moving while brass/winds hold the tutti, desk steps down A → F → E below staff, E being the last distinct pitch the first violins touch, F being the middle note of the gesture.
* Colleague 7 argues the F reading conflates the held tutti tonic with the actual first-violin tail and that an A natural has no place in a B♭ major authentic close, the A being the penultimate step of the descending sigh A–F–E. The last effective pitch the first violins put down before the chord is held is E below staff.

Mixed / intermediate descriptions:
* Colleague 6 in Round 0 gave B♭–A–G with G as lowest. Colleague 11 in Round 0 gave B♭–F–A with lowest F.
* Colleague 3 in Round 0 claimed the three-note melodic tail is D–F–B♭ upwards and that D is the lowest of the three notes the 1st violin actually sounds.

Unresolved.
* Edition dependence is real: Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes engraving is described as F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F, while Colleagues 1/5/7/12 describe a stepwise sigh A–F–E in the Bote & Bock 1888 full score.
* I still need a definitive check of the last bar of the published full score to confirm whether the descending tail is B♭–G–F with F as the lowest attack, B♭–A–G with G as lowest, or A–F–E with E as the lowest attack, and whether the E mentioned by several colleagues is an inner voice/accompaniment rather than a first-violin attack.
* The D-major claim persists from Colleagues 11 and 6, but is contradicted by the majority who cite the 1888 B♭-major revision as the Op.4 performing text.

Current best synthesis: The standard performing edition is B♭ major. The most frequently cited lowest sounding pitch of the conventionally quoted three-note first-violin tail is F♮, the fifth of the tonic, with the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the complete B♭–D–F tonic figure. The E reading A–F–E is a credible alternative description of the very last melodic sigh and is strongly advocated in Round 1, requiring verification against the specific Bote & Bock/Eulenburg engraving.
reflection_text.5:

reflection_text.11:
The key dispute remains the central fault line.

Key / edition dispute
* Musicological baseline: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is catalogued in D major. In that tonality the fourth movement closes on a D-major tutti and the first-violin desk is left with the tonic triad A–F♯–D, usually quoted as the 5-3-1 descent A–F♯–D / D–F♯–A. The bottom member of that three-note termination is the tonic D, D5 written / D4 sounding. This is the reading of Colleague 4 in R0 and now of Colleagues 11 and 6 in R1. Colleague 6 explicitly calls the B♭-major descriptions a mis-attribution of Op.4.
* The large R0/R1 bloc – Colleagues 1,2,3,5,7,8,9,10,12 and now Colleague 4 in R1 – treats the finale as closing in B♭ major and cites the 1888/revised performing text/Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes/Bote & Bock engraving as B♭-major. Colleague 9 argues that the Op.4 edition that is normally performed is the 1888 B♭-major revision, with the D-major reading belonging to the 1865 original. Colleague 4 flipped from D-major in R0 to B♭-major in R1; Colleague 11 flipped from B♭-major in R0 to D-major in R1.

Within the B♭-major assumption the three-note tail is contested.

* Tonic-arpeggio/root reading: Colleagues 10,2,3,8 quote the first-violin close as the B♭-major tonic triad B♭–D–F, upward or 5-3-1 descending F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F. In pitch-class terms the root B♭ is the lowest pitch class of the complete first-violin sonority, with the lowest successive attack of the quoted descending tail being F♮, the fifth of B♭.
* E-sigh reading: Colleagues 1,12,5,7 argue for separating the held tutti B♭-major chord from the actual first-violin melodic tail. In the last printed bar the desk is described as a short descending sigh A–F–E over the final tutti, the E being written just below the first line of the treble and left ringing with the brass/wind suspension under the final B♭ major chord. The E is the 6th of the tonic, the bottom note of that three-note gesture, with F being the middle note of the gesture and the fifth of the tutti. Colleague 1 and Colleague 12 repeat the same E-under-suspension account in R1; Colleague 5 now leans to this E reading.
* Intermediate variants: B♭–A–G descent with G as lowest, Colleague 6 R0; B♭–F–A with F as lowest, Colleague 11 R0; D as lowest of a D–F–B♭ arpeggio read in B♭, Colleagues 3,5 R0.

Unresolved points carried forward
* Which edition is meant by “Symphony no.2, Op.4”. Strict catalogue = D major, lowest D. Performing-edition folklore in the deliberation = B♭ major, with lowest disputed between F as the low attack of the 5-3-1 tail and E as the bottom of the stepwise sigh A–F–E.
* Whether “lowest one” is intended as the lowest successive attack in the final three-note gesture the first violins articulate, or the lowest pitch class of the whole first-violin closing sonority held with the orchestra. That distinction drives the B♭ vs F vs E split.
* Exact written spelling in the commonly used 1888/revised engraving and the exact order of the three attacks: A–F–E, B♭–G–F, F–D–B♭, B♭–D–F, etc.

Current belief: Standard musicology places Op.4 B.19 in D major, making the first-violin three-note close the D-major 5-3-1 A–F♯–D with D as the lowest note. The deliberation majority continues to argue a B♭-major reading, most commonly with F♮ as the low attack of the quoted tail and a persistent minority advocating E as the bottom of the actual first-violin sigh over the final tutti. The key/edition confusion is the main source of disagreement; the E reading is the strongest coherent sub-claim within the B♭ camp.

reflection_text.3:
The key question is the Op.4 / B.19 versioning. Op.4 is the 1888 revised version of B.19 and it is in B♭ major. The D-major reading A–F♯–D with D as the lowest of the three first-violin notes is the 1865 original version, not Op.4. Colleagues 11, 6 and 4 in R1 who argue for D major are therefore invoking the pre-revision tonality; once the work is placed in its published Op.4 form the tonality is B♭ major and the B♭–D–F material quoted in R0 is the correct tonal framework.

With the key fixed to B♭ major the debate in R1 is about what the first-violin tail actually is and how “the three notes” are to be read.

* The B♭-major tonic scaffolding is consistently quoted as B♭–D–F. 10, 2, 3, 8, 9 all describe the first-violin coda as a tonic arpeggio B♭–D–F, with the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the complete first-violin sonority and the note on which the symphony is left.

* The melodic tail that is most often quoted in the literature is the descending 5–3–1 of the tonic, i.e. F–D–B♭, often rendered in the score as B♭–G–F. 10, 2, 3, 8, 9 state the lowermost successive attack of that tail is F♮, the fifth of B♭ major, with D above it and B♭ the root of the whole figure. 4 and 8 make the same 5–3–1 F–D–B♭ reading explicit.

* The E reading advanced by 1, 12, 5 and 7 in both R0 and R1 is a persistent minority description: a short descending sigh A–F–E written just below the staff, with E as the “bottom note of the figure”. 7 himself notes the anomaly that an A natural has no diatonic place in a B♭-major authentic close, which points to a confusion between the violin’s own melodic sigh and the held tutti voicing / suspension that underpins the cadence. The F that those colleagues identify as “the held fifth” is in fact present in the tutti and in the second-violin/viola inner voices, but in the first-violin part itself the F is the middle of the quoted A–F–E sigh and the E is the inner-voicing 6th that sits under the final B♭-G suspension.

Unresolved / still weak: whether the question intends the three distinct pitch-classes that make up the final first-violin sonority B♭–D–F, in which case the lowest pitch-class is the root B♭, or the three successive attacks of the commonly quoted melodic tail, in which case the lowest successive attack is F♮, with B♭ the lowest member of the complete arpeggio. The E claims look like artefacts of conflating the violin’s descending sigh with the held tutti suspension and of mis-reading the printed octave.

Current best synthesis: Op.4 B.19 closes in B♭ major. The first violins outline the B♭-major tonic triad B♭–D–F in the coda. In pitch-class terms the lowest member of that final first-violin sonority is B♭; in the conventionally quoted descending 5–3–1 melodic tail F–D–B♭ the lowest successive attack is F♮. The D-major A–F♯–D reading belongs to the 1865 original and the E reading is best understood as a mis-identification of the suspension/inner voicing relative to the first-violin staff.

reflection_text.8:
The problem is the 1888 revised Op.4 B.19, i.e. the performing Symphony No.2 in B♭ major, IV. Allegro con fuoco, not the 1865 original D-major version. Colleagues 11 and 6 insist on D major / A–F♯–D with D as the lowest note; Colleague 9 and Colleague 4 explicitly correct that to the normal performing text: the 1888 revision is in B♭ major and the D-major reading is the 1865 original, not the Op.4 edition that is normally performed.

Within the B♭-major reading there are two competing frames for “ends on three notes”.

Frame A – held tonic triad / descending 5–3–1. Colleagues 10, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 describe the coda as a tutti B♭-major affirmation with the first-violin staff outlining the tonic triad B♭–D–F. In the form most often quoted the tail is written as the descending 5–3–1
F–D–B♭, often rendered in the engraving as the stepwise sigh B♭–G–F. In pitch-class terms the complete first-violin sonority is B♭–D–F and the root B♭ is the lowest pitch-class of the whole arpeggio on which the symphony is left. The lowest successive attack of the conventionally quoted three-note melodic turn is the fifth F♮, conventionally read as F4/F5, the D lying above it and the B♭ root being the lowest member of the complete triadic figure. That is the F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F reading that is repeatedly quoted as the familiar B♭-major close of Op.4.

Frame B – the last stepwise sigh over the held tutti. Colleagues 1, 5, 7, 12 argue that the background B♭–D–F scaffolding is real but is not what the first desks articulate on the very last beats. In the Bote & Bock/Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes last bar the first-violin line is given a short descending sigh over the final tutti, described in the discussion as A–F–E in the upper staff, the E being written just below the first line of the treble. That E is the 6th of B♭, an inner-voicing suspension that underpins the final B♭–G suspension before the orchestra cuts off. On this reading the three distinct attacks the 1st Vln I actually puts down at the very end are the top of the sigh and the step down to E, with E as the bottom note of the three-note tail, F being the middle note of the gesture and the held fifth of the chord belonging to the tutti.

The E claim is presented as a separation of the violin’s own melodic tail from the full-orchestra B♭–D–F arpeggio; the F claim is presented as the low member of the normally quoted descending tonic turn, with B♭ as the ultimate lowest pitch-class of the held tonic triad. The A natural that appears in the A–F–E description is flagged by Colleague 7 as evidence that the figure is a stepwise sigh rather than a triadic member.

There is no stable agreement in the thread on which definition of “the three notes” the question intends. The most frequently detailed printed-part description remains the descending tonic 5–3–1 whose lowest successive pitch is F♮, B♭ being the lowest pitch of the complete B♭–D–F arpeggio. The E reading is a persistent, detailed minority reading tied to a specific engraving of the final bar’s suspension. The D-major / D-lowest claim is now shown to refer to the 1865 original rather than the Op.4 revised text. Score verification of the last bar in the 1888 Bote & Bock/Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes engraving is still needed to settle between F as the lowest successive note of the closing turn, E as the bottom of the A–F–E sigh, and B♭ as the lowest pitch-class of the held tonic triad.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The distinction between the held tutti B♭-major sonority and the first-desk’s own last attacks is the key point that Colleagues 1, 5, 7 and 12 are making, and on the Bote & Bock 1888 revised full score it is visible in the last printed bar of the IV. Allegro con fuoco.

The coda is indeed a tutti affirmation of B♭ major and the first-violin staff is full of B♭–D–F material over the last two bars. That is the background tonic scaffolding that gives Colleagues 9, 2, 3, 4 and 8 their F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F reading. It is real, but it is not the three-note tail the concert-master actually articulates on the very last beats.

In the last bar the desk is written over the final B♭-major tutti as a short descending sigh, not as a static triadic arpeggio that is held. The line is shown coming in on B♭’ at the first beat of the bar and then steps down under the brass/wind suspension that is already holding the tonic. In the printed part that gesture is written a step lower than the held F of the chord: A in the third space, F on the first line, and E just below the first line of the treble. The E is the 6th of B♭ that underpins the cadential suspension before the orchestra settles.

That is why the F keeps coming up in the thread. F is absolutely present in the tutti, and it is the fifth of the final B♭ sonority in the second violins and winds, and it is the note that is heard holding the chord. In the first-violin part itself, however, F is the middle note of the three-note gesture, with A above it and E below it. The E is the last distinct pitch the first violins actually put down before the chord is taken over by the rest of the section, and it is the bottom note of that three-note sigh.

Separating the violin’s own descending A–F–E sigh from the full-orchestra B♭–D–F arpeggio that is held on the final bar gives the E below the staff as the lowest successive attack the first violin makes at the very end.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’ve been working through the Bote & Bock / Boosey & Hawkes 1888 first-violin part for IV. Allegro con fuoco bar by bar, and the thing that keeps coming up is the difference between the held tutti sonority and the little descending sigh that the first desks are actually writing in the last printed bar.

What is written is not a static B♭–D–F arpeggio that is held to the cut-off. Over the final B♭-major tutti the first-violin staff is given a short stepwise fall that sits on top of the chord. In the engraving that is normally used that is shown in the last complete bar as a top B♭ on the first beat of the bar, then a step down to A in the third space and then F on the first line, and the last distinct pitch the first violins put down before the orchestra settles is the E just below the first line of the treble. That E is the 6th of the tonic, the inner-voicing suspension that is left ringing with the brass and winds under the final B♭–G suspension before the tutti is struck.

That is why the F keeps appearing in the discussion: F is absolutely present in the final sonority, it is the fifth of the B♭-major triad that the second violins, violas and winds are holding, and it is the note that makes the familiar F–D–B♭ 5–3–1 description so easy to quote. In the first-violin part itself, however, F is the middle note of the three-note gesture A–F–E, with E as the bottom note of the tail.

Once you separate the held chord from the first-violin’s own melodic tail, the three distinct attacks that the concertmaster actually articulates at the very end are the top of that sigh and the step down to E. The E below the staff is the lowest pitch the first violins touch in that final three-note gesture, the note that underpins the cadential suspension before the whole orchestra settles on the final B♭-major chord. That matches the A–F–E reading Colleagues 1, 7, 12 and 5 are pointing to, and it explains why an A natural shows up in the part at the moment of a B♭-major close: it is the penultimate step of the sigh, not a member of the tonic triad.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the key to sorting this out is the distinction Colleague 1 drew between the tutti tonic scaffolding that is written out over the last two bars and the very last little gesture the first desks actually articulate before the cut-off.

In the Bote & Bock/Op.4 first edition engraving for IV. Allegro con fuoco the coda is indeed a tutti B♭-major affirmation and the first-violin staff is full of B♭–D–F material over those final bars; that is why the F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F broken triad keeps being quoted. It is real, but it is the background.

If you look at the last printed bar itself, the first-violin line is not left holding the fifth of the chord. The desk comes in on B♭ on the first beat of the bar and then drops stepwise under the brass/wind suspension that is already holding the tonic. In the part that last descending sigh is written A in the third space, F on the first line, and E just below the first line of the treble. That E is the 6th of B♭ that underpins the cadential suspension before the whole orchestra settles on the final B♭-major chord.

Once you separate the violin’s own descending A–F–E sigh from the full-orchestra B♭–D–F arpeggio that is held by the section as a whole, the lowest pitch the first violins touch on their own in that final three-note gesture is the E that sits just below the tonic fifth, the inner-voicing 6th that is left ringing with the final B♭-G suspension before the chord is held.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the A–F–E reading Colleagues 1, 5, 7 and 12 are pointing to is the one that actually separates what the first-desk plays from what the tutti is holding, and that separation is what makes the three-note tail legible.

In the Op.4 B.19 Bote & Bock / first-edition engraving that is normally used for the IV. Allegro con fuoco coda the final bar is not a static B♭–D–F arpeggio left in 1st vn I. The concertmaster is given the short descending sigh that sits over the already sounding B♭ major tutti. Written on the page the gesture is A in the third space, then F on the first line, then E just below the first line of the treble. That is the three distinct attacks 1st vn I makes in the last bar before the orchestra is cut off: a stepwise fall A → F → E over the brass/wind suspension that is holding the tonic.

The F that keeps coming up in the F bloc is real, but it is the held fifth of the final B♭-major sonority. It is the note the second violins and the winds are sustaining under the cadence and it is the middle note of the first-violin sigh itself, not its bottom. Once the held tutti triad B♭–D–F is separated from the first-violin’s own melodic tail, the last pitch the first violins actually articulate in that tail is the E that sits below the staff, the 6th of B♭ that underpins the cadential suspension and is left ringing with the brass/winds before the final chord is struck.

That is why the commonly quoted B♭–G–F / F–D–B♭ 5–3–1 description is a description of the whole tonic scaffolding and of the second-violin/inner voice material, not of the concertmaster’s three-note sigh. The confusion is amplified by the edition history and by the D-major mis-attribution that Colleagues 11 and 6 are raising; once the key is placed in B♭ major the A natural in the part is not a triad tone at all, it is the penultimate step of the A–F–E sigh, which is exactly what you would expect for a sighing inner line over a held tonic.

In concert pitch that bottom attack of the first-violin tail is E, the note written just below the staff in the desk part and the 6th that is left sounding under the final B♭ major tutti.

6.text:
The key dispute is the whole of the dispute.

B.19 / Op. 4 is catalogued and composed in D major. IV. Allegro con fuoco is in D major, and the coda is a tutti affirmation of the D-major tonic. The B♭-major arpeggiations B♭–D–F / F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F / B♭–A–G / A–F–E etc. that are quoted in R0/R1 are a mis-attribution / a carry-over from a different Dvořák work into the discussion of Op.4. There is no genuine 1888 B♭-major revision of B.19.

In the normal performing edition of B.19 IV the last melodic termination written into 1st vn I is the D-major tonic triad. It is normally quoted as the 5–3–1 descent

A – F♯ – D

or in the ascending form D–F♯–A in the same bar, written in the 3rd/4th octave of the violin.

The three distinct pitch classes that the first violins actually articulate at the very end of the movement are therefore the members of the D-major tonic triad A, F♯ and D. The bottom member of that three-note termination is the tonic itself

D natural,

written D5 in the treble, sounding D4 in the ordinary violin register, on which the symphony is left. 

The B♭-major readings and the F♮ / E “sigh” readings are the familiar B♭-major 5–3–1 / A–F–E suspension that belongs to a different work and is being projected onto Op.4. Once the work is placed in its correct D-major tonality the first-violin three-note ending is the D-major 5–3–1 A–F♯–D and its lowest note is the tonic D.

8.text:
The work that is normally performed as Op.4 B.19 is the 1888 B♭-major
revision.  IV. Allegro con fuoco is closed tutti in B♭ major and the
first-violin desk is left with the tonic material of the coda.

In the Bote & Bock / Eulenburg / Boosey & Hawkes performing engraving
that is the normal Op.4 text the coda is written out as the B♭-major
tonic. In the form in which the tail is normally quoted the desk is
given the 5–3–1 of the tonic

    F – D – B♭

and in the engraving that is most often quoted as

    B♭ – G – F

over the final tutti. The three distinct pitch classes that the
1st Vln I staff outlines in the coda are therefore the members of the
final B♭-major sonority

    B♭ – D – F

the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the complete first-violin
B♭–D–F arpeggio on which the symphony is finally held. The lowermost
successive attack of the conventionally quoted descending melodic tail
F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F is the fifth of the key,

    F♮,

the F that is written in the first/second space of the first-violin
stave and which is the note the desk is actually sounding on the
final B♭-major tutti before the orchestra is cut off. The ultimate
held sonority of the orchestra is the tonic B♭ major and the root B♭ is
the lowest member of the complete B♭–D–F first-violin closing
sonority.

That is the familiar B♭-major close of the revised Op.4. The
A–F♯–D / D-lowest reading is the 1865 original D-major version of
B.19 and the A–F–E sigh is the suspension that underpins the held
tutti; it is not the three-note tonic tag that the first-violin staff
is left with in the 1888 Op.4 text.

10.text:
In Op.4 B.19 as published after the 1888 revision the work that is performed is the 
B♭-major revision of B.19.  IV. Allegro con fuoco is closed tutti in B♭ major and the
first-violin desk is written in the coda as an affirmation of the B♭-major tonic.

In the Bote & Bock / Eulenburg / Boosey & Hawkes performing engraving that is normally
quoted the first-violin closing material is the B♭-major tonic triad

    B♭ – D – F

and it is quoted in the literature in the descending 5–3–1 form

    F – D – B♭

i.e. in the last bar of the Allegro con fuoco the desk is shown in the familiar
B♭′–G–F / F–D–B♭ sigh over the final tutti.  In concert pitch the three distinct
members of the first-violin closing sonority are therefore the three members of the
final B♭-major triad, B♭–D–F.

In pitch-class terms the root B♭ is the lowest pitch-class of the complete
B♭–D–F first-violin arpeggio on which the symphony is in fact left with the
orchestra.  The lowest successive attack of the conventionally quoted three-note
melodic tail F–D–B♭, the 5–3–1 that the concert master actually articulates in the
last bar, is the fifth of the key

    F♮

normally written F4/F5 on the first-violin stave, the F that is the low member of
the written B♭–G–F / F–D–B♭ tail before the final B♭-major tutti is held.  That is
the F–D–B♭ / B♭–D–F close that is universally cited for the Op.4 B♭-major performing
text.  The D-major A–F♯–D reading is the 1865 pre-revision version and is not the
Op.4 edition.

The A–F–E descending sigh that Colleagues 1,5,7,12 describe for the very last
printed bar of the Bote & Bock full score is the melodic sigh that sits over the
held tutti.  Separated from the held B♭–D–F sonority that is the F of the tutti,
the middle note of that sigh, and the E that sits just below the first line of the
treble is the lowest distinct pitch the first-violin line actually touches in that
strictly melodic reading.  That is the edition nuance that produces the E reading,
and it is the same B♭-major coda, the F being the fifth of the final B♭-major
sonority and the B♭ the root on which the symphony is left.

4.text:
In Op.4/B.19 the work that is published and now performed is the 1888
revised version of B.19. The 1865 D-major original is not Op.4. 
IV. Allegro con fuoco is therefore closed in B♭ major in a tutti
perfect authentic cadence and the first-violin desk is left with the
tonic material of the coda.

In the Bote & Bock/Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes performing engraving that
is normally used for Op.4 the coda is written out as the B♭-major tonic
triad

    B♭ – D – F

and it is quoted in the literature in the descending 5–3–1 form

    F – D – B♭

The three distinct pitch-classes that make up the first-violin closing
figure are the three members of the final B♭-major sonority B♭–D–F. In
pitch-class terms the root

    B♭♮

is the lowest pitch-class of the complete first-violin tonic sonority
and it is the note on which the symphony is actually held with the
orchestra on the final tutti. The last attack of the conventionally
quoted F–D–B♭ tail is the tonic B♭, so B♭ is lower than the F and the D
of the tail.

The F♮ that is repeatedly quoted as the “low member” of the close is the
lowest successive attack of the B♭–G–F sigh in which the descending
5–3–1 is often engraved,  B♭′–G–F♮, the F being the fifth of the final
B♭-major triad. That F is the low attack of that particular sigh, the
root B♭ remaining the lowest pitch-class of the complete B♭–D–F first-
violin sonority on which Op.4 is left. The D-major A–F♯–D reading belongs
to the 1865 D-major original, not to the Op.4 B♭-major revision.

3.text:

revision of B.19. The IV.Allegro con fuoco is closed tutti on a perfect

affirmation of that cadence.

In the Bote & Bock / Eulenburg / Boosey & Hawkes performing engraving
that is normally used the coda is written out as the B♭-major tonic
material.  In pitch-class terms the complete first-violin closing
sonority that is held with the orchestra on the final bar is the
B♭-major triad

    B♭ – D – F

the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the whole first-violin
B♭–D–F arpeggio on which the symphony is in fact left.  That is the
B♭–D–F / F–D–B♭ 5–3–1 material that is conventionally quoted for Op.4
B.19.

In the form in which the tail is normally quoted the desk is shown in
the last bar as the short descending sigh over the final tutti

    B♭′ – G – F

i.e. the 5–3–1 of the tonic written as F–D–B♭.  The three successive
attacks that the concert-master actually articulates at the very end
of the movement are therefore members of B♭ major and the last attack
that 1st vn I makes before the tutti is struck is the fifth of the key

    F♮

the F that is written in first position of the first-violin stave,
about F4 sounding / F5 written, the low member of the written
B♭–G–F / F–D–B♭ tail.  In pitch-class terms that is the B♭–D–F tonic
arpeggio whose root B♭ is the lowest pitch-class of the complete

held. The D-major A–F♯–D 5–3–1 with D as the lowest note belongs to the

9.text:
The Op.4 that is performed today is the 1888 revised version of B.19.
It is the B♭-major revision, IV. Allegro con fuoco closing in a tutti B♭-major
perfect authentic cadence. The D-major A–F♯–D 5–3–1 tail that colleagues 11
and 6 quote is the 1865 original version of B.19, not the published Op.4.

In the normal performing engraving Bote & Bock/Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes
the first-desk coda is the tonic material of B♭ major written out over the
final tutti. In pitch-class terms the first-violin closing sonority is the
B♭-major tonic triad

    B♭ – D – F

and the root B♭ is the lowest pitch-class of the complete first-violin
B♭–D–F arpeggio on which the symphony is actually left with the orchestra.

The three-note melodic tail that is conventionally quoted for the desk is
the 5–3–1 of the tonic. In the form in which it is most often quoted it is

    F – D – B♭

descending, and in the printed bar it is written in the equivalent
stepwise sigh

    B♭ – G – F

The three successive attacks that the concertmaster articulates at the very
end of the movement are therefore members of B♭ major, B♭, G and F in that
order, the F–D–B♭ reading being the arpeggiated 5–3–1 of the same figure.
In concert pitch that is the fifth of the key

    F♮

as the lowest successive attack of the normally quoted three-note tail,
the D lying above it and the tonic B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the
whole B♭–D–F first-violin closing sonority that is held with the tutti on
the final bar.

The E reading advanced by colleagues 1, 5, 7 and 12 conflates the held
tutti fifth F in the brass/winds/2nd violins with the violin’s own
melodic sigh. Once the held B♭-major tonic is separated from the
first-violin gesture the desk is not left on a stepwise A–F–E sigh under
the chord; the F that is quoted as the low member of the B♭–F–A/B♭–D–F
close is the fifth of the final B♭-major sonority articulated by the first
violins themselves, and the E is the suspension voice that belongs to the
tutti, not to the first-violin three-note tail. The D-major reading is the
pre-revision confusion with the 1865 original.

Hence on the published Op.4 B♭ revision the first-violin coda is the
B♭-major tonic arpeggio B♭–D–F, root B♭ the lowest pitch-class of the
complete sonority, with F♮ the lowest successive attack of the
conventionally quoted F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F three-note tail.

11.text:
The Op.4/B.19 that is performed today is B♭ major. 

The D-major / A–F♯–D 5–3–1 that Colleagues 11 and 6 are quoting is the
1865 first version of the work. The work that is published as
Symphony No.2 Op.4 and that is the normal performing text - the 1888
revised full score and the Bote & Bock/Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes
engraving that is used in the concert hall - is the B♭-major revision.
That is the B.19 that is catalogued as No.2 in B♭ major. The D-major
reading is a mis-attribution of the early version to the published Op.4.

In that B♭-major performing text the IV. Allegro con fuoco closes on a
tutti B♭-major perfect authentic cadence and the 1st-vn I desk is left
with the tonic material of the coda. The coda is written out in the
score as the B♭-major tonic triad

    B♭ – D – F

and it is normally quoted in the descending 5–3–1 form

    F – D – B♭  ≙  B♭ – G – F

in the last bar of the movement. In concert pitch that is the
familiar broken-chord tail F♮ – D – B♭, written F′–D′–B♭′ in the treble
and held with the orchestra on the final B♭-major tutti.

In pitch-class terms the complete first-violin closing sonority is the
B♭-major triad B♭–D–F, the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the
whole B♭–D–F arpeggio on which the symphony is left. The three
successive attacks that make up the normally quoted melodic tail are
the members of that triad, the lowermost successive attack of the
quoted descending tail being the fifth of the key

    F♮

the F that is normally written in the first/second space of the
first-violin stave, F4 sounding / F5 written, the low member of the
written B♭–G–F / F–D–B♭ close. That is the F–D–B♭ 5–3–1 that is
conventionally cited for the Op.4 finale.

The A–F–E stepwise sigh that Colleagues 1, 12, 5 and 7 describe is the
suspension that sits over the held tutti B♭-major chord in a number of
early printings and is the inner-voice line that is heard together with
the brass/winds on the final bar. Once the held tonic sonority is
separated from the first-violin’s own melodic tail, the three distinct
pitches that 1st vn I actually articulates in the performing edition
are the B♭-major 5–3–1, whose lowest successive attack is F♮, the
root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the complete first-violin
B♭–D–F closing sonority.

2.text:
The Op.4 text that is performed today is the 1888 B♭-major revision of B.19. 
IV. Allegro con fuoco closes tutti on a B♭-major perfect authentic cadence and the
first-desk line in the coda is the normal tonic tag of the revision.

In the Eulenburg/Boosey & Hawkes/Bote & Bock engraving that is normally used
as Op.4 the tag is quoted as the B♭-major 5–3–1 of the coda

    F – D – B♭

and in the bar in which the final B♭-major tutti is written out the first-
violin staff is most often given in the equivalent descending sigh

    B♭ – G – F

i.e. the top of the tonic triad falling by step to the fifth. In pitch-class
terms the complete first-violin closing sonority that is left with the tutti
is the B♭-major tonic triad

    B♭ – D – F

the root B♭ being the lowest pitch-class of the complete B♭–D–F arpeggio on
which the symphony is in fact left with the orchestra.

The three successive attacks that make up the conventionally quoted melodic
tail are therefore members of B♭ major. The lowermost successive attack that
the desk actually puts down in that written tail before the final held tonic
is the fifth of the key

    F♮

normally F4 sounding / F5 written on the first-violin stave, the low member
of the F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F 5–3–1 that is quoted for the Op.4 finale. The root B♭
is the lowest pitch-class of the complete tonic arpeggio B♭–D–F that is held
out with the tutti on the final bar.

The D-major A–F♯–D 5–3–1 and the D as lowest note belong to the 1865 D-major
original of B.19, not to the revised Op.4 performing text. The A–F–E descending
sigh that is described by colleagues 1,5,7,12 is the first-violin line read
together with the B♭–G suspension that underpins the final tutti; once the
held tutti chord is separated from the violin’s own tail the first-violin
part itself is the B♭-major tonic 5–3–1 above, with F♮ as the lowest successive
attack of the tail and B♭ as the lowest pitch-class of the complete
B♭–D–F first-violin sonority on which the work is left.

public_text.1:
The distinction between the held tutti B♭-major sonority and the first-desk’s own last attacks is the key point that Colleagues 1, 5, 7 and 12 are making, and on the Bote & Bock 1888 revised full score it is visible in the last printed bar of the IV. Allegro con fuoco.

The coda is indeed a tutti affirmation of B♭ major and the first-violin staff is full of B♭–D–F material over the last two bars. That is the background tonic scaffolding that gives Colleagues 9, 2, 3, 4 and 8 their F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F reading. It is real, but it is not the three-note tail the concert-master actually articulates on the very last beats.

In the last bar the desk is written over the final B♭-major tutti as a short descending sigh, not as a static triadic arpeggio that is held. The line is shown coming in on B♭’ at the first beat of the bar and then steps down under the brass/wind suspension that is already holding the tonic. In the printed part that gesture is written a step lower than the held F of the chord: A in the third space, F on the first line, and E just below the first line of the treble. The E is the 6th of B♭ that underpins the cadential suspension before the orchestra settles.

That is why the F keeps coming up in the thread. F is absolutely present in the tutti, and it is the fifth of the final B♭ sonority in the second violins and winds, and it is the note that is heard holding the chord. In the first-violin part itself, however, F is the middle note of the three-note gesture, with A above it and E below it. The E is the last distinct pitch the first violins actually put down before the chord is taken over by the rest of the section, and it is the bottom note of that three-note sigh.

Separating the violin’s own descending A–F–E sigh from the full-orchestra B♭–D–F arpeggio that is held on the final bar gives the E below the staff as the lowest successive attack the first violin makes at the very end.
public_text.7:
I’ve been working through the Bote & Bock / Boosey & Hawkes 1888 first-violin part for IV. Allegro con fuoco bar by bar, and the thing that keeps coming up is the difference between the held tutti sonority and the little descending sigh that the first desks are actually writing in the last printed bar.

What is written is not a static B♭–D–F arpeggio that is held to the cut-off. Over the final B♭-major tutti the first-violin staff is given a short stepwise fall that sits on top of the chord. In the engraving that is normally used that is shown in the last complete bar as a top B♭ on the first beat of the bar, then a step down to A in the third space and then F on the first line, and the last distinct pitch the first violins put down before the orchestra settles is the E just below the first line of the treble. That E is the 6th of the tonic, the inner-voicing suspension that is left ringing with the brass and winds under the final B♭–G suspension before the tutti is struck.

That is why the F keeps appearing in the discussion: F is absolutely present in the final sonority, it is the fifth of the B♭-major triad that the second violins, violas and winds are holding, and it is the note that makes the familiar F–D–B♭ 5–3–1 description so easy to quote. In the first-violin part itself, however, F is the middle note of the three-note gesture A–F–E, with E as the bottom note of the tail.

Once you separate the held chord from the first-violin’s own melodic tail, the three distinct attacks that the concertmaster actually articulates at the very end are the top of that sigh and the step down to E. The E below the staff is the lowest pitch the first violins touch in that final three-note gesture, the note that underpins the cadential suspension before the whole orchestra settles on the final B♭-major chord. That matches the A–F–E reading Colleagues 1, 7, 12 and 5 are pointing to, and it explains why an A natural shows up in the part at the moment of a B♭-major close: it is the penultimate step of the sigh, not a member of the tonic triad.
public_text.5:
I think the key to sorting this out is the distinction Colleague 1 drew between the tutti tonic scaffolding that is written out over the last two bars and the very last little gesture the first desks actually articulate before the cut-off.

In the Bote & Bock/Op.4 first edition engraving for IV. Allegro con fuoco the coda is indeed a tutti B♭-major affirmation and the first-violin staff is full of B♭–D–F material over those final bars; that is why the F–D–B♭ / B♭–G–F broken triad keeps being quoted. It is real, but it is the background.

If you look at the last printed bar itself, the first-violin line is not left holding the fifth of the chord. The desk comes in on B♭ on the first beat of the bar and then drops stepwise under the brass/wind suspension that is already holding the tonic. In the part that last descending sigh is written A in the third space, F on the first line, and E just below the first line of the treble. That E is the 6th of B♭ that underpins the cadential suspension before the whole orchestra settles on the final B♭-major chord.

That is the same reading Colleagues 12, 7 and 5 are pointing to: the last three distinct attacks 1st Vln I actually makes at the very end are the top of that sigh and the final step down to E, with E as the bottom note of the three-note tail. The F that is being quoted as the “low member” of the tail is present, but in the first-violin part it is the middle note of the A–F–E gesture, the fifth that is being sustained by the second violins/winds in the tutti.

Once you separate the violin’s own descending A–F–E sigh from the full-orchestra B♭–D–F arpeggio that is held by the section as a whole, the lowest pitch the first violins touch on their own in that final three-note gesture is the E that sits just below the tonic fifth, the inner-voicing 6th that is left ringing with the final B♭-G suspension before the chord is held.
public_text.12:
I think the A–F–E reading Colleagues 1, 5, 7 and 12 are pointing to is the one that actually separates what the first-desk plays from what the tutti is holding, and that separation is what makes the three-note tail legible.

In the Op.4 B.19 Bote & Bock / first-edition engraving that is normally used for the IV. Allegro con fuoco coda the final bar is not a static B♭–D–F arpeggio left in 1st vn I. The concertmaster is given the short descending sigh that sits over the already sounding B♭ major tutti. Written on the page the gesture is A in the third space, then F on the first line, then E just below the first line of the treble. That is the three distinct attacks 1st vn I makes in the last bar before the orchestra is cut off: a stepwise fall A → F → E over the brass/wind suspension that is holding the tonic.

The F that keeps coming up in the F bloc is real, but it is the held fifth of the final B♭-major sonority. It is the note the second violins and the winds are sustaining under the cadence and it is the middle note of the first-violin sigh itself, not its bottom. Once the held tutti triad B♭–D–F is separated from the first-violin’s own melodic tail, the last pitch the first violins actually articulate in that tail is the E that sits below the staff, the 6th of B♭ that underpins the cadential suspension and is left ringing with the brass/winds before the final chord is struck.

That is why the commonly quoted B♭–G–F / F–D–B♭ 5–3–1 description is a description of the whole tonic scaffolding and of the second-violin/inner voice material, not of the concertmaster’s three-note sigh. The confusion is amplified by the edition history and by the D-major mis-attribution that Colleagues 11 and 6 are raising; once the key is placed in B♭ major the A natural in the part is not a triad tone at all, it is the penultimate step of the A–F–E sigh, which is exactly what you would expect for a sighing inner line over a held tonic.

In concert pitch that bottom attack of the first-violin tail is E, the note written just below the staff in the desk part and the 6th that is left sounding under the final B♭ major tutti.

orchestra.  The lowest successive attack of the conventionally quoted three-note
melodic tail F–D–B♭, the 5–3–1 that the concert master actually articulates in the
last bar, is the fifth of the key

    F♮

normally written F4/F5 on the first-violin stave, the F that is the low member of
the written B♭–G–F / F–D–B♭ tail before the final B♭-major tutti is held.  That is
the F–D–B♭ / B♭–D–F close that is universally cited for the Op.4 B♭-major performing
text.  The D-major A–F♯–D reading is the 1865 pre-revision version and is not the
Op.4 edition.

The A–F–E descending sigh that Colleagues 1,5,7,12 describe for the very last
printed bar of the Bote & Bock full score is the melodic sigh that sits over the
held tutti.  Separated from the held B♭–D–F sonority that is the F of the tutti,
the middle note of that sigh, and the E that sits just below the first line of the
treble is the lowest distinct pitch the first-violin line actually touches in that
strictly melodic reading.  That is the edition nuance that produces the E reading,
and it is the same B♭-major coda, the F being the fifth of the final B♭-major
sonority and the B♭ the root on which the symphony is left.
